$$

q-335450.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(-1) \\ y(-1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
q-335450.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-(-1))}\,x(-1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-337109.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$  Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}.
q-337109.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L3 and L4. Starting from L3, x(t)=eAtc, we evaluate both sides at t=t0 to obtain x(t0)=eAt0c which is line L4. Therefore, L4 follows from L3 by substituting t=t0.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Line L5 gives (eAt0)−1x(t0)=(eAt0)−1eAt0c. Since (eAt0)−1eAt0=In, the right-hand side simplifies to c, so c=(eAt0)−1x(t0). Simplify once, then apply (eAt0)−1=e−At0, to obtain c=e−At0x(t0), which is line L6. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by the fact that (eAt0)−1=e−At0.
